slides.title: Threat actors
points: Threat actors differ in goals, resources, access, and capability. Security+ expects you to recognize who is most likely behind a scenario.
Security+ Objective 2.1: compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations.

slides.title: Nation-state
slides.teach: A government-backed or government-aligned threat actor that may conduct cyber operations for intelligence, military, political, or strategic objectives.

course.learn: A government-backed or government-aligned threat actor that may conduct cyber operations for intelligence, military, political, or strategic objectives.

breakdown.explanation: Think a country or state-backed group with significant resources and long-term goals.
Espionage, Critical infrastructure targeting, Long-term campaigns

course.why: Nation-state actors may have substantial funding, patience, intelligence support, and access to advanced capabilities.
course.example: A foreign government-linked group quietly steals defense research over several years.
course.check_q: Which actor is most associated with state sponsorship and strategic geopolitical goals?

slides.title: Unskilled attacker
slides.teach: An attacker with limited technical skill who relies heavily on existing tools, scripts, or public exploits.

course.learn: An attacker with limited technical skill who relies heavily on existing tools, scripts, or public exploits.

breakdown.explanation: Prebuilt exploit kits, Copied attack scripts, Public scanning tools

course.why: These attackers may still cause damage even without advanced capability because powerful tools are widely available.
course.example: A teenager launches a public exploit script against exposed systems without understanding the underlying vulnerability.
course.exam: Limited skill + downloaded tools → UNSKILLED ATTACKER.
course.check_q: Which actor typically relies most on public tools and copied scripts?

slides.title: Hacktivist
slides.teach: An attacker or group motivated primarily by a social, political, or ideological cause.

course.learn: An attacker or group motivated primarily by a social, political, or ideological cause.

breakdown.explanation: Website defacement, Data leaks, DDoS for a cause

course.why: The goal is usually publicity, protest, disruption, or advancing a cause rather than simple financial gain.
course.example: A group defaces a company website to protest the company's political position.
course.check_q: Which actor is most associated with political or philosophical causes?

slides.title: Insider threat
slides.teach: A person with legitimate access who intentionally or accidentally creates security risk.

course.learn: A person with legitimate access who intentionally or accidentally creates security risk.

breakdown.explanation: The person is already inside the organization or already trusted.
Malicious employee, Careless administrator, Departing employee stealing data

course.why: Insiders can bypass some external defenses because they already possess legitimate access, knowledge, or trust.
course.example: An employee exports customer records before resigning.
course.exam: Already has legitimate access → INSIDER THREAT.
course.check_q: Which actor already has legitimate organizational access?

slides.title: Organized crime
slides.teach: A coordinated criminal group that uses cybercrime for profit or other criminal objectives.

course.learn: A coordinated criminal group that uses cybercrime for profit or other criminal objectives.

breakdown.explanation: Think professional cybercrime run like a business.
Ransomware groups, Fraud rings, Credential theft operations

course.why: Organized groups can fund infrastructure, specialize roles, and scale attacks for financial return.
course.example: A ransomware group operates affiliates, payment infrastructure, and support channels to extort hundreds of organizations.
course.exam: Profit + coordinated criminal operation → ORGANIZED CRIME.
course.check_q: Which actor is most associated with coordinated, scalable cybercrime for profit?

slides.title: Shadow IT
slides.teach: Technology, services, or systems used without formal approval or oversight from the organization’s IT or security team.

course.learn: Technology, services, or systems used without formal approval or oversight from the organization’s IT or security team.

breakdown.explanation: Employees use technology the organization did not approve.
Unsanctioned cloud storage, Unapproved SaaS, Personal devices used for business

course.why: Unapproved technology can bypass security controls, logging, data governance, and compliance requirements.
course.example: Employees upload confidential company files to an unapproved cloud-storage service because it is easier to use.
course.check_q: What term describes business technology used without IT approval?

hero.title: Threat actors
hero.intro: Threat actors differ in goals, resources, access, and capability. Security+ expects you to recognize who is most likely behind a scenario.

blocks.title: Threat actors
blocks.prompt: Compare the clues in the scenario and identify the most likely actor, attribute, or motivation.

cards.name: Nation-state
cards.definition: A government-backed or government-aligned threat actor that may conduct cyber operations for intelligence, military, political, or strategic objectives.

cards.name: Unskilled attacker
cards.definition: An attacker with limited technical skill who relies heavily on existing tools, scripts, or public exploits.

cards.name: Hacktivist
cards.definition: An attacker or group motivated primarily by a social, political, or ideological cause.

cards.name: Insider threat
cards.definition: A person with legitimate access who intentionally or accidentally creates security risk.

cards.name: Organized crime
cards.definition: A coordinated criminal group that uses cybercrime for profit or other criminal objectives.

cards.name: Shadow IT
cards.definition: Technology, services, or systems used without formal approval or oversight from the organization’s IT or security team.

blocks.title: Identify the actor from the clues
items: Government resources + long-term strategic goal → Nation-state
Nation-state actors are commonly associated with significant resources, patience, and strategic objectives.
Example: A foreign government-linked group steals defense research over several years.
Limited skill + downloaded tools → Unskilled attacker
The actor relies on existing scripts or tools rather than advanced custom capability.
Example: A teenager launches a public exploit script against exposed systems.
The attack is tied to political, social, or philosophical beliefs.
Example: A group defaces a website to promote a political message.
Already has legitimate access → Insider threat
The actor is inside the organization or already has authorized access.
Example: An employee exports customer records before resigning.
Profit + coordinated criminal operation → Organized crime
Organized criminal groups commonly pursue scalable financial gain.
Example: A ransomware group encrypts hundreds of organizations for payment.
The risk comes from technology used without IT/security approval or governance.
Example: Employees upload company files to an unsanctioned cloud-storage service.
blocks.example: Memory: Nation-state = government · Unskilled = public tools · Hacktivist = cause · Insider = access · Organized crime = profit · Shadow IT = unapproved tech.

questions.q: A foreign government-linked group spends years stealing defense research and avoids detection using custom tools. Which threat actor is most likely?
questions.explanation: Nation-state actors are associated with state sponsorship, strategic goals, significant resources, and long-term operations.

questions.q: An attacker with little technical knowledge launches a public exploit script exactly as downloaded from the internet. Which actor best fits?
questions.explanation: Unskilled attackers commonly rely on public scripts and ready-made tools.

questions.q: A group launches a DDoS attack to protest a company’s political position. Which threat actor is most likely?
questions.explanation: Hacktivists are primarily motivated by political, social, or ideological causes.

questions.q: An employee with legitimate database access copies customer information before resigning. Which threat actor is this?
questions.explanation: The employee already has legitimate internal access, making this an insider threat.

questions.q: A coordinated ransomware group uses affiliates, payment infrastructure, and specialized teams to extort victims for money. Which actor best fits?
questions.explanation: Organized crime groups often run coordinated cybercrime operations for profit.

questions.q: Employees begin using an unapproved cloud-storage service to share company files without IT approval. What is this?
questions.explanation: Shadow IT is technology used without formal IT or security approval.

questions.q: Which actor is most likely to have significant government funding and geopolitical objectives?
questions.explanation: Nation-state actors are typically associated with government backing and strategic geopolitical goals.

questions.q: Which actor category can include both malicious employees and careless authorized users?
questions.explanation: Insider threats include intentional and accidental risks created by people with legitimate access.
